title: The Sabbath - time with God
summary: The Sabbath was instituted already at creation, for all people, as a memorial of the Creator and a weekly gift of relationship and freedom. The fourth commandment, which Jesus himself kept, leads to rest in Christ - not a burden, but a space to meet with God.

sections.heading: A Gift Older Than Israel: the Sabbath at Creation

items.comment: After six days God rests, blesses, and sanctifies the seventh day. This happens in Eden - for all of humanity, long before Israel or any religion existed.

questions.text: Since the Sabbath appears already at creation, who was it actually meant for?

items.label: "the seventh day" (yôm haššᵉbîʿî / šabbāt)
items.content: In Gen 2:2-3 and Exod 20:10 it speaks of "the seventh day" (*yôm haššᵉbîʿî*); the noun *šabbāt* comes from a root meaning "to cease, to stop." The biblical week counts the days from the first (Sunday) to the seventh (Saturday) - the Sabbath is consistently the last, seventh day, and not the first.

questions.text: How does the biblical counting of days (first = Sunday, seventh = Saturday) help establish which day the commandment is about?

items.label: the verb "rested" (šābaṯ) in the creation account
items.content: In Gen 2:2-3 the noun *šabbāt* does not yet appear; instead, the verb *šābaṯ* ("to cease, to stop") occurs twice to describe God's rest after the work of creation. The heart of it, then, is not relief from tiredness, but a deliberate CEASING from finished work - God blessed this day (*bārak*) and sanctified it (*qādaš*), that is, "set it apart" for a lasting purpose.

questions.text: What changes in how we see the Sabbath when we see in it a "ceasing" from finished work, and not just a remedy for tiredness?

items.comment: Jesus says: "The Sabbath was made for man." It is a gift for people, not a burden laid on them - and Jesus is its Lord.

questions.text: What changes when we see the Sabbath as "for man" rather than "against man"?

items.comment: God teaches the people Sabbath rest through the manna - even BEFORE Sinai. The Sabbath is not an "invention" of the Ten Commandments; the Ten Commandments only confirm it.

questions.text: What does it teach us that God introduces the Sabbath before he wrote down the Ten Commandments?

items.label: the first use of the noun *šabbāt*
items.content: It is precisely in the manna account (Exod 16) that the noun *šabbāt* appears for the first time in the entire Old Testament (four times). God's words, "See, the LORD has given you the Sabbath," and the rebuke, "How long will you refuse?" assume that the Sabbath was ALREADY known to the people, and not just then being instituted. This further confirms its roots reaching back to creation.

sections.heading: The Fourth Commandment and Remembrance of the Creator

items.comment: The only commandment that begins with "Remember." The reason is clear: because God created everything in six days, and on the seventh he rested. The Sabbath is a weekly memorial that I have a Creator.

questions.text: What is the word "Remember" at the start of this commandment meant to guard against?

items.label: "Remember" (zākar)
items.content: The verb *zākar* ("remember") opens the fourth commandment, the only one to do so. It can carry several shades at once: to remember something already long established, to remember because there is a danger of forgetting, and to remember with the future in mind - because the Sabbath remains ever relevant for the covenant. The language of the whole commandment (six days of work, seventh of rest, the blessing and sanctifying of the day) directly summarizes Gen 2:2-3.

questions.text: Which shade of the word "remember" speaks most to your situation - memory of the past, a warning against forgetting, or a look toward the future?

items.label: the Sabbath as the "seal" of the Ten Commandments
items.content: In antiquity a complete seal contained three elements: the name, the title (office), and the domain of authority of its owner. The fourth commandment is the only one in the Ten Commandments that gives all three: the name ("the LORD your God"), the office (Creator - "made"), and the domain of authority ("heaven and earth, the sea and all that is in them"). That is why it is sometimes called the "seal" of God's law, confirming whose authority stands behind the whole of the Ten Commandments.

items.comment: God calls the Sabbath a "sign" between him and his people - a sign that it is he who sanctifies. The Sabbath is a sign of relationship, of who knows whom.

questions.text: Of what is the Sabbath meant to be a sign according to this text - our effort or God's action?

items.label: the Sabbath as a "sign" and "everlasting covenant" (Exod 31:13, 17)
items.content: In Exod 31:13-17 the Sabbath is a "sign" with a double dimension: that it is God who sanctifies his people (v. 13) and that he is the Creator (v. 17). The text also calls it an "everlasting covenant" (v. 16) and says that after creating, God "was refreshed" - not from tiredness, but as a joyful satisfaction after finished, perfect work. The Hebrew "to know" that "I am the LORD" means above all a close relationship, not merely knowledge.

questions.text: How does "knowing" God as a close relationship differ from mere knowledge about him - and how does the Sabbath build that relationship?

items.comment: The Sabbath is described as a "delight," a day turned away from one's own affairs and rushing about. It is an invitation to joy, not to petty prohibitions.

questions.text: What would it mean to experience the Sabbath as a "delight," rather than as a list of "you must not"?

items.comment: The final call of the gospel rings out: "Worship him who made heaven and earth." The language directly echoes the fourth commandment - the Sabbath connects with the appeal to acknowledge the Creator.

questions.text: Why, at the close of history, is it precisely the call to worship the Creator that returns?

items.comment: "As was his custom," Jesus went to the synagogue on the Sabbath. If we want to live as Jesus did, it is worth noticing what his custom was regarding this day.

questions.text: What does Jesus' custom tell us about his attitude toward the Sabbath?

items.comment: Jesus heals on the Sabbath and defends it: it is a day for setting people free from bondage, not a day of dead prohibitions. He cleanses the Sabbath of human burdens, rather than abolishing it.

questions.text: What does Jesus "repair" in the understanding of the Sabbath, and what does he not remove?

items.label: the disputes were over tradition, not over the commandment
items.content: Jesus' disputes about the Sabbath did not concern things forbidden in the Old Testament, but the "oral law" - an elaborate rabbinic tradition (later written down in the Mishnah), which enumerated 39 main classes of "work" and a host of petty prohibitions. Jesus did not break Scripture, but restored the day's original, inner meaning, cleansing it of human burdens. What comes under criticism, then, is distorted TEACHING, not the Sabbath itself.

questions.text: How do you distinguish God's commandment about the Sabbath from the human traditions that grew up around it over time?

items.comment: Speaking of events after his departure (the destruction of Jerusalem some forty years later), Jesus still assumes that the Sabbath will matter to his disciples. He does not foretell its disappearance.

questions.text: What follows from the fact that Jesus speaks of the Sabbath as still important after his departure?

items.comment: Jesus invites the weary: "Come, and I will give you rest." The outward Sabbath points to a deeper rest - a ceasing from the effort of trying to earn our place.

questions.text: From what "carrying" does Jesus want to free us by offering rest?

items.comment: "There remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God" - whoever has entered this rest has rested from their own works, as God did from his. The Sabbath becomes a picture of salvation by grace, not by works.

questions.text: How can a weekly rest teach the truth that salvation is a gift, not a reward?

items.label: "Sabbath rest" (sabbatismos)
items.content: In Heb 4:9 a rare Greek word appears, *sabbatismos* ("Sabbath rest"), used only once in the New Testament. Throughout the whole passage (Heb 3:7-4:13) the noun *katapausis* ("rest") also appears eight times. The author's argument makes sense only if the recipients are still keeping the weekly Sabbath - the day becomes for them a picture of a deeper, spiritual rest in Christ.

questions.text: How can an outward day of rest point to an inner "rest of faith" in Christ?

items.comment: One enters God's rest through faith. An outward day without inward trust remains empty - but one does not exclude the other.

questions.text: What is "entering rest through faith" as distinct from merely having a day off?

items.comment: After the death of Jesus the women "rested according to the commandment" on the Sabbath (Saturday), and after it, on "the first day of the week" (Sunday), they went to the tomb. The text itself distinguishes the two days - the seventh is the day of rest in keeping with the commandment.

questions.text: Which day does the Gospel writer call the day of rest "according to the commandment," and which an ordinary working day?

items.label: Sunday gatherings in the New Testament
items.content: The texts cited in favor of Sunday (e.g. Acts 20:7 - breaking bread on the first day of the week; 1 Cor 16:2 - setting aside gifts) describe single gatherings or the practice of collecting an offering, but they do not establish a new holy day or abolish the fourth commandment. What is more, the gathering in Acts 20:7 was a nighttime meeting (by biblical reckoning, Saturday evening), and the offering in 1 Cor 16:2 was to be set aside at home, not in the congregation. These texts contain no language of command or of transferring the holiness of the day.

items.comment: "As was his custom," Paul teaches on the Sabbaths - many years after the resurrection. In the New Testament there is no command to transfer the day of rest to another day.

questions.text: If the holy day had been officially changed, what would you expect to find in the New Testament, and what is missing?

items.label: the historical change of the day of worship
items.content: The New Testament contains no command to transfer rest from the seventh day to the first; nor is there any trace in it of a controversy over the Sabbath - whereas every serious change in religious practice (such as the dispute over circumcision) left a clear trace. The widespread keeping of Sunday took hold gradually in the first centuries of the church and was confirmed by later church and imperial decisions (among them Constantine's edict of 321 concerning the "venerable day of the sun," which nonetheless permitted agricultural work that was forbidden on the Sabbath of the Pentateuch). From the perspective of sola scriptura, this is a change introduced by human tradition, not by a biblical command. Note: we evaluate the teaching and decisions of institutions, never the sincerity of individual believers, many of whom worship God on Sunday in good faith.

application.text: The Sabbath is not a Jewish relic or a burden of prohibitions. It is a gift older than Israel - instituted in Eden for every human being, a weekly memorial that I have a Creator, to whom I belong. Jesus kept it and freed it from human burdens. Every week the Sabbath invites me to stop proving my worth through work and achievement, and to rest in the One who already loves me. The outward rest points to the deepest one - rest in Christ, salvation by grace, not by works.
application.challenge: Plan the coming seventh day (Saturday) deliberately as a day of relationship, not of duties: set aside work and hurry, find time for the Bible, prayer, loved ones, and nature. Afterward write one sentence: what did you discover about God when you stopped "producing"?
